blocks.text: Several statements in this chapter need careful boundaries. James connects conflicts among the hearers with desires at war within them and with asking directed toward self-indulgence; this does not make people who suffer violence responsible for it or require them to remain in abuse. “Friendship with the world” names disloyal alignment in this context, not rejection of creation, human bodies, cultures, or non-Christians. “Double-minded” describes divided loyalty in James, rather than mental illness, neurodivergence, doubt, or seeking help. Verse 5 is especially difficult: its syntax, whether it quotes Scripture, and what “spirit” refers to are all disputed, so translations may legitimately differ. In verses 11–12, speaking against and judging a sibling is connected with judging the law and taking the place of the one lawgiver and judge; this warning does not cancel accountability, survivor testimony, legal protection, or community processes for addressing harm. The merchants in verses 13–17 are rebuked for presuming control over tomorrow and profit, not for planning itself; the passage cautions against boastful certainty rather than commending fatalism.
James does not name Jerusalem or any other place as its place of composition. The book itself therefore does not provide a specific location from which to explain this chapter.
